This notebook shows how to draw landscapes, choose species parameters, run a
Geonomics simulation, and retrieve genetic and spatial data for your own analyses.
It is a reusable workflow for a simulation-based final project. You supply the
research question, landscape design, parameter comparisons, and analyses.

The workflow is **draw → configure → simulate → inspect → analyze**. Shiny is
used only for drawing. Geonomics runs the simulation in Python; you work with
its inputs and outputs in R.

## 1. Open the project and load the tools

On DataHub, open `Landscape_Simulation_HowTo.Rproj` in RStudio, then open this
Rmd. Keep `support/` beside the Rmd. Opening the project sets the working directory
so the relative file paths below work.

Run chunks individually, in order, for your first pass. Drawing requires your
interaction, so do not start with Knit or Run All.

```{r setup}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, cache=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=7)

# If needed, install these once in the R console:
# install.packages(c("shiny", "jsonlite", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))

source("support/notebook_helpers.R")
Sys.setenv(EVODOODLE_PYTHON="/srv/conda/envs/notebook/bin/python")
```

These helpers use DataHub's Python environment with Geonomics already installed.
You do not need to import Python into R with reticulate or install the Python
Evodoodle package.

## 2. Draw three landscape layers

Each layer is a matrix with one number per cell. All three layers describe the
same area and must have the same dimensions.

| Layer | Role | Meaning of the values |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Carrying capacity | Spatial variation in population capacity | 0 = no capacity; 1 = maximum relative capacity |
| Connectivity | Surface used to guide movement | Low values = low connectivity; high values = high connectivity |
| Environment | Local optimum for the selected trait | 0 to 1 = different local trait optima, rather than better or worse habitat |

In this model, connectivity guides movement directions; a zero cell is not a
guarantee of an impermeable barrier. For a project about barriers, distinguish
movement preference from habitat capacity and check that the simulation produces
the intended movement pattern.

The next chunk opens all three maps together. Select **0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, or 1**
below a map, then click or drag to paint. Brush selections are independent for each
map. Fresh maps begin at 1 everywhere. Click **Save all and return to notebook**
when all layers are ready.

```{r draw-landscapes}
landscapes <- draw_landscapes(
  d = 10,
  title = "Draw your project landscapes",
  file = "landscapes/project_landscapes.rds"
)
```

`d = 10` creates a 10 × 10 grid. After Save, the editor stops; a disconnected
editor page is normal. Return to RStudio. The object `landscapes` is a named list
of three R matrices, and a copy is saved on disk.

```{r inspect-landscapes}
carrying_capacity <- landscapes$carrying_capacity
connectivity <- landscapes$connectivity
environment <- landscapes$environment

plot_landscapes(carrying_capacity, connectivity, environment)
dim(carrying_capacity)
```

To reopen and edit your maps, use the following optional chunk. It edits a copy
and saves it under a new filename. Enable the chunk or run its code manually.

```{r edit-landscapes, eval=FALSE}
landscapes_edited <- draw_landscapes(
  initial = landscapes,
  title = "Edit a copy of your landscapes",
  file = "landscapes/project_landscapes_edited.rds"
)
```

You can also inspect or edit a matrix directly in R. For example,
`carrying_capacity[3, 5]` is the cell in row 3, column 5. Rows increase downward
from the top of the maps; columns increase to the right. To use an edited set in
a simulation, pass that set's matrices to `run_geonomics()`.

## 3. Construct the parameters object

`gnx_parameters()` builds a named R list containing the settings exposed by this
wrapper. Edit its arguments before running a simulation. For an interpretable
comparison, first change one parameter or landscape feature at a time.

```{r choose-parameters}
params <- gnx_parameters(
  phi = 0.05,               # Selection strength: 0 to 1
  n_loci = 1,               # Loci controlling the selected trait: 1 to 100
  K_factor = 5,             # Capacity per cell at capacity-layer value 1
  movement_distance = 0.5,  # Movement-distance distribution parameter (>0)
  mating_radius = 4,        # Maximum mate-search distance in cell widths (>0)
  seed = 154                # Positive integer random seed
)
```

| Argument | How to interpret or change it |
|:--|:--|
| `phi` | Larger values strengthen selection toward the local environmental optimum; 0 removes selection on this trait. |
| `n_loci` | Number of loci underlying the selected trait. This is separate from the total genomic loci. |
| `K_factor` | Multiplies the carrying-capacity layer. A cell with value 0.5 and `K_factor = 5` has nominal capacity 2.5; realized abundance fluctuates. |
| `movement_distance` | Changes the movement-distance distribution; larger values increase its scale in this template. It is not a guaranteed distance for each individual. |
| `mating_radius` | Sets the distance within which individuals can find mates. |
| `seed` | Controls random number generation. Use different seeds for independent replicate runs. |

The template uses **1,000 total genomic loci** and **500 starting individuals
before burn-in**. Burn-in lets the demographic population settle before genomic
initialization and the main simulation. The population present at main step 0 can
therefore differ from 500. The number of individuals is not held constant.
These two template settings are not arguments to `gnx_parameters()`.

Display the settings you are about to use. The table reads the two fixed values
from the actual template so they cannot silently disagree with the file.

```{r display-parameters}
template <- jsonlite::fromJSON("support/model_params.json", simplifyVector=FALSE)
species_settings <- template$comm$species$spp_0

parameter_table <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c(
    "Starting individuals (before burn-in)", "Total genomic loci",
    "Selection strength", "Loci controlling the selected trait",
    "Carrying-capacity multiplier", "Movement distance",
    "Mating radius", "Random seed"
  ),
  Value = c(
    species_settings$init$N, species_settings$gen_arch$L,
    params$phi, params$n_loci, params$K_factor,
    params$movement_distance, params$mating_radius, params$seed
  )
)
knitr::kable(parameter_table, row.names=FALSE)
```

For example, `phi = 0.1` increases selection strength relative to 0.05;
`K_factor = 3` lowers nominal capacity relative to 5. Rerun the parameter and
table chunks after edits. Existing saved simulations retain their original inputs.

## 4. Submit a model run to Geonomics

This chunk passes the three matrices and `params` to the Python runner. It
constructs a new model, completes demographic burn-in, and then runs two
consecutive 100-step stages of the **same population**.

```{r run-simulation}
mod <- run_geonomics(
  carrying_capacity = carrying_capacity,
  connectivity = connectivity,
  environment = environment,
  params = params,
  steps = c(100, 100),
  name = "project_example"
)
```

Wait for the chunk to finish. RStudio will be busy; Shiny is already closed.
Run one simulation at a time. The console prints the path to the Python log.
The helper waits for Python and then returns a small R result object, `mod`.
It contains saved data and paths, not a live Python model.

`steps = c(100, 100)` saves stages at main steps **0, 100, and 200**. Step 0 is
after burn-in. Use `steps = 200` for only stages 0 and 1 (steps 0 and 200), or
`steps = c(50, 50, 50)` for stages 0 through 3 (steps 0, 50, 100, 150).

Each new `run_geonomics()` call constructs a fresh population. It does not
continue a previous `mod`. Put all successive stages of a run in `steps`.
Names may contain letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens. Use descriptive,
unique names to keep scenarios and replicates identifiable.

```{r run-summary}
mod$folder
knitr::kable(mod$stages, row.names=FALSE)
```

The summary reports population size and mean observed heterozygosity across all
loci, including fixed loci, at each saved stage.

## 5. Inspect the simulation

```{r plot-initial}
plot_popgen(mod, stage=0)
```

```{r plot-final}
plot_popgen(mod, stage=2)
```

The four panels show genetic PCA, individuals on the landscape colored by their
PC scores, individual heterozygosity, and phenotype against the local environment.
The last panel uses the same scale for phenotype and environment. PCA is fitted
separately at each stage: signs and RGB colors can change, so do not interpret a
color change between stages alone as a biological change. Quantitative analyses
should accompany visual comparisons in a final project.

## 6. Retrieve VCFs and coordinates

The model saves genetic and spatial data at every stage, not just the final one.

| File | Contents |
|:--|:--|
| `stage_XX.vcf` | Diploid genotypes for all individuals and all loci, including fixed sites |
| `stage_XX_coordinates.csv` | Individual ID and x/y coordinates |
| `stage_XX_individuals.csv` | ID, coordinates, phenotype, and observed heterozygosity |
| `stage_XX_dosage.csv.gz` | Individual-by-locus allele dosage matrix used by the plotting helpers |
| `stages.csv` | Stage numbers, cumulative main steps, abundance, and mean heterozygosity |
| `result.rds` | Saved R result object for reopening the run |

For this two-stage example, `stage_02` is the final population at step 200.
Determine the final stage from the summary rather than hard-coding it in reusable
project scripts:

```{r retrieve-outputs}
final_stage <- max(mod$stages$stage)
prefix <- file.path(mod$folder, sprintf("stage_%02d", final_stage))

vcf_file <- paste0(prefix, ".vcf")
coordinates <- read.csv(paste0(prefix, "_coordinates.csv"))
individuals <- read.csv(paste0(prefix, "_individuals.csv"))

vcf_file
head(coordinates)
head(individuals)
```

The coordinates are in **simulation grid units**, not longitude/latitude. Match
individuals by sample ID when combining VCFs and coordinates, rather than assuming
their orders are identical. ID values identify individuals; they do not guarantee
that the same individuals survive across stages. Keep each stage's paired files
together. Fixed loci are retained in the VCF; filter them when your chosen analysis
requires polymorphic loci.

Use the Files pane in RStudio to navigate to `mod$folder` and download files with
Export, or read them directly into the R tools you already use. For example, if
you choose to use **vcfR**, the following optional code imports the VCF:

```{r import-vcf, eval=FALSE}
# Install vcfR once if needed: install.packages("vcfR")
vcf <- vcfR::read.vcfR(vcf_file, verbose=FALSE)
```

## 7. Design comparisons and replicates

For a project, define a response (for example, diversity, differentiation, or
trait–environment matching), the factor you will manipulate, and the conditions
you will hold constant. Use several independent seeds per treatment to distinguish
a treatment effect from stochastic variation. Keep the same run length and output
stages when comparing treatments unless time itself is the factor of interest.

Below is an optional pattern for three replicates of the current landscape. Enable
it only when you are ready to run three additional full simulations. Each finishes
before the next starts; choose new names when changing the design.

```{r replicate-example, eval=FALSE}
seeds <- c(201, 202, 203)
replicates <- lapply(seeds, function(s) {
  replicate_params <- gnx_parameters(
    phi=params$phi, n_loci=params$n_loci, K_factor=params$K_factor,
    movement_distance=params$movement_distance,
    mating_radius=params$mating_radius, seed=s
  )
  run_geonomics(
    carrying_capacity, connectivity, environment,
    params=replicate_params, steps=c(100,100),
    name=paste0("baseline_seed_",s), rerun=TRUE
  )
})
```

To compare landscapes, draw and save a second named set, then pass its matrices
to another run with the same biological parameters and an appropriate seed plan.
Record the landscape files, parameter settings, seeds, run length, and analyses
so someone else can reproduce your project.

## 8. Save and reopen your work

Drawings are already saved under `landscapes/`; each run is saved under `runs/`.
Keep those folders with your project locally and in your submission. The included
`.gitignore` excludes them from Git to keep generated data out of the code repository;
use your course's submission method to share the data.

These optional commands restore existing objects without drawing or simulating:

```{r reopen-example, eval=FALSE}
landscapes <- readRDS("landscapes/project_landscapes.rds")
mod <- readRDS("runs/project_example/result.rds")
plot_popgen(mod)  # Defaults to the last saved stage
```

Rerunning a drawing chunk normally opens the editor again; `redraw=FALSE` reuses
its saved file. Rerunning a simulation chunk interactively normally launches a new
run in a new folder; `rerun=FALSE` reuses the latest saved result for that name.
Reuse loads old inputs and outputs: it does not apply edits to your current matrices
or parameters. On a repeat run, `mod$folder` identifies the actual numbered folder.

After completing the interactive chunks, Knit/Preview reuses your own saved
landscapes and simulation results. Optional chunks marked `eval=FALSE` are shown
but not executed when rendering. Keep them disabled for a simple introductory run.

If a simulation reports an error, read the log named in the console. If a population
goes extinct, review habitat capacity and biological settings. Begin with the
10 × 10 grid, 1,000 loci, and default density that have been tested on DataHub;
larger populations or genomes increase computational demand. The VCF export is a
new addition and should be checked with a fresh run in your DataHub environment.
